title: Time, Tense, and Aspect: Three Different Things
brief: Open by establishing that time, tense, and aspect are three distinct concepts that learners and teachers routinely conflate. Define time as a universal concept (past, present, future) that exists independently of language. Define tense as a grammatical category realised by changes to the verb form itself — English has exactly two morphological tenses, past and present. Define aspect as the way a verb form presents the internal shape or structure of an event (whether it is ongoing, completed, habitual, etc.). Use short invented example sentences such as 'She walks to work' versus 'She walked to work' to show tense at work, and contrast 'She was walking' with 'She walked' to show aspect at work within the same time frame. Stress that understanding these three layers separately is essential for teachers who need to explain grammar accurately rather than relying on misleading labels.

title: English Has Only Two Tenses — and Why That Matters
brief: Explain that English marks tense morphologically on the verb in only two ways: the base/present form (walk, writes) and the past form (walked, wrote). There is no inflectional future tense in English — no suffix or ending that marks futurity the way -ed marks the past. Show this with a clear invented paradigm: 'I work / I worked' versus the impossibility of a single-word inflected future like 'I work-tomorrow.' Explain that future time is instead expressed through modal constructions (will/shall), the semi-modal 'be going to,' the present continuous, and the simple present with a future time adverbial — all of which are grammatical structures, not tenses. Clarify that calling 'will + infinitive' the future tense is a convenient but technically inaccurate label that can confuse learners when they encounter the many other ways English expresses future time. Keep the explanation grounded in verb morphology and avoid straying into detailed modal semantics, which belong in a later unit.

title: Simple and Continuous Aspect
brief: Introduce aspect as the grammatical feature that tells us how a speaker chooses to present an event or state — not when it happens, but what shape it has. Explain the simple aspect first: it presents an action or state as a whole, without internal structure, and is used for habits, facts, completed actions, and sequences. Invent examples such as 'The train leaves at six' and 'He painted the fence.' Then explain the continuous (progressive) aspect, formed with be + -ing, which presents an action as ongoing, in progress, or temporary at a reference point in time. Invent contrasting pairs such as 'I read the report' (simple — completed) versus 'I was reading the report when the phone rang' (continuous — in progress at a past moment). Describe a simple timeline in words: imagine a horizontal line representing time; the continuous aspect zooms in on a stretch of that line and shows the action unfolding across it, while the simple aspect treats the same event as a single point. Note that stative verbs (know, believe, contain) do not normally take the continuous, and give a brief invented example to illustrate.

title: Perfect and Perfect Continuous Aspect
brief: Explain the perfect aspect, formed with have + past participle, which creates a connection between two points in time — typically linking a past event to a present (or later) reference point. Use invented examples: 'She has finished the report' (present perfect — the finishing is in the past but relevant now) versus 'She finished the report' (simple past — the event is located in the past with no explicit link to now). Describe the timeline in words: picture two points on the time line; the perfect aspect draws a bridge between them, signalling that the earlier event has current relevance or that a period of time has elapsed. Then introduce the perfect continuous aspect (have + been + -ing), which combines both features: it shows an activity that began earlier and has been ongoing up to the reference point, often with present results or evidence. Invent an example such as 'He has been running — look how tired he is' and contrast it with 'He has run five kilometres today' (perfect simple, focusing on the completed quantity). Clarify that the choice between perfect simple and perfect continuous often signals whether the speaker emphasises completion or ongoing duration.

title: Combining Tense and Aspect: The Full Grid
brief: Bring tense and aspect together by showing how the two tenses (present and past) combine with the four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) to produce the eight core verb forms that describe real time across past, present, and future. Present this as a logical system rather than a list of twelve or sixteen 'tenses' to memorise. Use a small invented set of sentences built around one scenario — for example, a character named Mia and her work on a project — to show how the same event can be framed differently depending on tense and aspect choice: 'Mia works on the project' / 'Mia is working on the project' / 'Mia has worked on the project' / 'Mia has been working on the project' / and their past equivalents. Explain that future time slots into this system through modal and periphrastic structures that carry their own aspectual meanings (will be working, will have finished). Emphasise to the teacher-reader that presenting grammar as a system of meaningful choices — rather than a catalogue of forms — helps learners understand why a particular form is used, not just how to produce it.

title: Classroom Implications: Teaching the System, Not the Label
brief: Draw together the unit's key points and translate them into practical awareness for the TEFL teacher. Stress that accurate metalanguage matters: a teacher who understands that 'future tense' is a convenient shorthand, not a morphological reality, will be better equipped to handle learner questions such as why 'I'm meeting Dan tonight' can express future time. Recommend that teachers present tense and aspect as a system of choices driven by meaning — what the speaker wants to communicate about the shape, duration, or relevance of an event — rather than as a set of rules to be drilled in isolation. Suggest using invented minimal pairs in the classroom (two sentences identical except for the verb form) to draw learners' attention to the meaning difference aspect creates, for example 'I lived in Rome' versus 'I have lived in Rome.' Close by reminding teachers that learners whose first languages mark tense or aspect differently — or not at all — will need explicit, accurate explanation of how the English system works, making the conceptual clarity developed in this unit directly useful in the classroom.
